title: Technical Trust Slate: Dedicated Capacity for Enterprise Buyers
body:
Purpose:
This slate provides a concise but technical-friendly narrative and procurement-ready artifacts for enterprise buyers evaluating dedicated capacity. Focus is on signals of operational trust: predictable throughput, isolation guarantees, quantifiable SLAs, and engineering controls buyers rely on when assessing vendor risk.

Primary audience:
- Platform architects and SRE leads evaluating capacity contracts
- Procurement teams drafting RFPs and SLA language
- Security/compliance reviewers validating isolation controls

One-line positioning:
Dedicated Redwood capacity: contractable inference throughput with built-in isolation and engineering-enforced fallbacks so platform teams can trade model economics for business certainty.

Core value pillars (short bullets buyers care about):
- Predictable unit economics: throughput commitments mapped to per-token pricing bands and volumetric credits to avoid surprise bill variability.
- Isolation by policy: dedicated GPU pools, network boundaries, key management integrations, and optional lockbox for sensitive workloads.
- Measurable SLAs: tail-latency and availability SLOs with clear crediting and remediation steps.
- Operational transparency: token-level telemetry, route tracing, and incident blameless postmortems accessible to named contacts.

Supporting proof points (what engineering can cite in scoping calls):
- Serving runtime: continuous batching and KV cache management reduce predictable per-token compute variance by up to X% (provide benchmark links in final copy).
- Kernel selection and quantization profiles: model-specific profiles allow consistent throughput across model versions under committed capacity.
- Smart routing and fallback: automated model variants and regional fallbacks with contractable latency windows.

Buyer-focused message map (short — use in slides/one-pagers):
- For Platform Teams: "Guaranteed slots, clear fallbacks, predictable cost per request when traffic is mission-critical."
- For Security/Compliance: "Separable control plane, private VPC option, KMS/HSM keys, audit logs and support for SOC2/ISO artifacts."
- For Procurement: "Template clauses for throughput credits, SLA credits, termination for chronic SLO breach, and capacity ramp milestones."

Competitive differentiators to call out versus cloud-managed endpoints or self-hosted stacks:
- Unified experience across hosted, dedicated, private: same API and operational tooling simplifies vendor lock-in risk.
- Run-time optimizations tuned for production distributions (not research benchmarks) — we optimize for steady-state throughput and tail latency at scale.
- Procurement-friendly contract constructs: burst buffers, predictable scaling ladders, and clear crediting math (not open-ended throttles).

Procurement-ready artifacts (copy/paste friendly snippets below):
1) Availability and latency SLA (excerpt):
"Provider shall maintain a monthly availability of 99.9% for dedicated capacity endpoints. Availability is defined as the percentage of 1-minute windows in which the endpoint can accept and begin processing requests. For Tail Latency, 99th percentile end-to-end latency for requests of standard payload size must not exceed 500ms. Failure to meet monthly availability or tail latency guarantees entitles Customer to SLA credits as specified in section X."

2) Isolation assurance clause (excerpt):
"Dedicated Capacity Isolation: Provider will allocate isolated GPU pools for Customer workloads. These pools will not be shared with non-Customer tenants. Provider shall provide documentation of tenancy boundaries, network ACLs, and KMS key scoping. Any maintenance operations impacting isolation will be communicated 72 hours in advance except for emergency remediation."

3) Throughput and burst policy (excerpt):
"Committed Throughput: Provider agrees to reserve N concurrent inference slots or an equivalent token-per-second throughput metric. Burst Buffer: Provider will allow bursts up to 2x committed throughput for up to 10 minutes per hour, with automated throttling only after burst allowance is consumed. Provider will supply route-level metrics and alerting thresholds for contract monitoring."

4) Remediation and escalation (excerpt):
"Upon material SLA breach, Provider will: (a) supply a written incident report within 72 hours; (b) provision a remediation plan with timelines within 10 business days; (c) provide financial credits per schedule. Chronic breaches (3 breaches in 6 months) permit Customer to terminate without penalty and receive a pro-rata refund of committed fees for the remaining term."

Operational controls & signals to make visible in procurement demos:
- Slot utilization dashboards and historic capacity charts (7, 30, 90 day views)
- Per-route token-cost and latency heatmaps
- Incident history with MTTR and root-cause tags
- Isolation evidence: tenancy mapping, VPC peering diagrams, KMS usage logs

Objection handling (quick bullets for field reps):
- "Why not just run ourselves?" => "Self-hosting shifts OS/infra/serving runtime ops and removes our SLO-backed commitments plus cost predictability; Redwood combines optimized runtime with contractable economics and 24/7 support for production inference."
- "How do you guarantee isolation?" => "Dedicated GPU pools + network segmentation + optional private control plane and audited maintenance windows; we provide artifacts and live tenancy mapping during procurement."
- "What if model changes break throughput?" => "We offer model onboarding gates, quantization profiles, and pre-cutover canary timeframes; throughput guarantees apply to vetted model artifacts and config profiles."

Suggested internal asks for pre-sales to collect during discovery calls:
- Expected steady-state RPS and peak concurrency windows
- Typical request payload sizes and percent of streaming vs. single-call workloads
- Compliance controls required (e.g., SOC2, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
- Desired contract term and rollback/termination conditions
- Preferred regions and data residency constraints

Quick procurement readiness checklist (one-liners to attach to proposals):
- Templated SLA language drafted? Yes/No
- Isolation evidence package prepared? Yes/No
- Agreed throughput metric and measurement method? Yes/No
- Ramp milestones and penalty schedule defined? Yes/No
- Named technical contact for incident reviews? Yes/No

Next steps / recommended owner actions:
- Sales engineering: run a short "technical trust" demo focusing on dashboards above and tenant isolation artifacts. (Owner: Liam O'Connor)
- Legal: vet template clauses for crediting math and termination rights. (Owner: Priya Singh)
- Product: finalize benchmark artifacts for committed-profile claims and attach quantization caveats. (Owner: Maya Chen)

Notes and open questions (to iterate in follow-ups):
- Decide exact burst buffer sizing and crediting formula for different SKU tiers.
- Define metrics for measuring "begin processing" for availability calculations (edge cases for queued requests).
- Determine whether emergency maintenance notification window can remain at 72 hours for regulated buyers.

Appendix: quick metrics primers for procurement teams (copy-friendly)
- Availability: percent of 1-minute windows with successful acceptance of new requests.
- Tail latency: 95th/99th percentile full request lifecycle from client TCP handshake to final token emitted.
- MTTR: mean time to return to committed throughput after a capacity-impacting incident.

End of slate. Use this doc as the technical backbone for one-pagers, procurement attachments, and scoping templates.
